requested.title: Untagged image-request decoder + attacker-chosen AAD lets a server-island props token be replayed as an image request (SSRF with response reflection)
readVarint overflows to NaN, silently defeating the length bounds check
Security-relevant numeric image options are accepted unvalidated while every neighbouring field throws on bad input
The documented "cacheDir must NOT be under publicDir" constraint is never enforced, so a misconfiguration publishes cached originals
Source fetch buffers the whole body in memory with no concurrency or total-cache cap, on a route that bypasses the rate limiter
Upstream response bodies are left un-cancelled on three throw paths in the redirect/validation loop
Image token AAD lacks a purpose label, so tokens minted for other payload types are accepted and their plaintext drives an outbound fetch
No output-pixel budget: a single-dimension size amplifies an extreme-aspect-ratio source into an unbounded allocation

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: I traced the whole chain and every link holds at HEAD. (1) The route: `Mochi.ts:1707` registers `${assetPrefix}/image/:filename` directly into `bunRoutes` via `withHead(...)`. Bun dispatches `routes` before `fetch`, and `buildRequestContext` is never called, so there is no `checkRouteLimit`, no `csrfCheck`, no `protection` gate (confirmed: `protectionRuntime.gate` is only wired into `publicRouteGuard` at Mochi.ts:1845 and the fetch fallback at 1898) and no `KIND_POLICY` entry — `RouteKind` has no `image` member at all. It is mounted by default (`enabled: o.enabled ?? true`). (2) The AAD is wholly attacker-chosen: `imageEndpoint.ts:74` is `url.pathname.split('/').pop() ?? ''` with zero validation, handed straight to `decryptImageRequest(token, filename)` (L82), which passes it as `aad` to `decryptPayloadBytes`. (3) One key for everything: `payloadCrypto.sivKey()` is `HMAC-SHA512(secretKey, 'mochi-payload-aes-siv-v1')` memoized per secret — image requests, island props, captcha and clearance all use it, and the AAD string is the only domain separator. (4) `unpackImageRequest` has no magic/version/type tag; it reads `control = buf[0]` and otherwise returns a request for essentially any byte string. (5) The island side matches: `svelteAstPreprocess.ts` (both the visible and non-visible defer branches) emits `component-name="${islandKey}" signed-props={__mochi_encrypt_props__(__mochi_stringify__(envelope), "islandKey")}`, and `islandIdentity()` guarantees `islandKey` is `<Name>_<base36 hash>` — a bare `\w+` token, i.e. a legal single path segment. `shouldInlineIsland()` returns false on an ordinary page render, so the placeholder with `signed-props` really does land in the HTML. (6) `stringify` is devalue's (`mochi-framework.d.ts` re-exports it); I read `node_modules/devalue/src/stringify.js` and confirmed an object root serializes as `[{"k":1,...},"v1",...]`, so byte 0 = 0x5B (= ORIGINAL|HAS_SIZE|HTTP_PREFIX — 91 has bits 0,1,3 set and bit 2 clear) and byte 1 = 0x7B = 123, making `nameLen` 123 and `src = 'http://' + plaintext.slice(125)` exactly as described. Because `original` is set, `getSize` is skipped, `getCachedOriginal(src)` runs, and the upstream bytes are returned in the response body (lines 96-114) — `safeOriginalContentType` only forces `application/octet-stream`/`attachment` for non-raster types, it does not withhold the bytes. Concrete self-service attack on a default config: an app with `<Child mochi:defer query={q} />` where `q` comes from the query string; the envelope devalues to `[{"query":1,"islandId":2},"<USER>","s1-0"]`, putting the user string's first byte at offset 27, so `?q=` + 98 filler chars + `attacker.com/` places the host at offset 125. The attacker loads that page themselves, copies `signed-props` out of their own HTML, and GETs `/_mochi/image/<islandKey>?p=<token>` — the server fetches `http://attacker.com/<remainder of the sealed plaintext>` and hands the response body back. `allowedHosts` defaults to undefined so any public host is reachable; deflate compression is transparent (inflate restores the exact plaintext); the offset is deterministic and trivially binary-searched off the 400-vs-403 difference. That breaks two guarantees the project states explicitly: `packages/docs/148-images.md` line 17 ("an attacker cannot request arbitrary sources or transforms") and the Callout at ~line 92 that recommends `mochi:defer` precisely because its props are encrypted — the tail of the plaintext (later props) is exfiltrated into the attacker's access log. The ancillary claims also check out: `warnUnknownSize(request.size)` does fire (request.size is the 123-byte garbage, `size` is undefined) and `warnedUnknownSize` is an unbounded module-level Set. The only sub-claim I had to correct is the clearance oracle: `PROTECTION_AAD` plaintext is `{"iat":...,"bits":N}` (~31 bytes), so `2 + 34 > 31` makes `unpackImageRequest` return null and the response is the same 403 as a failed decrypt — no oracle there. The captcha oracle does work (its plaintext is ~78 bytes, past the offset, so a genuine token yields 400 'Invalid source URL' vs 403 'Invalid payload'), though its practical value is low since the attacker is handed valid captcha tokens anyway. HIGH stands on the SSRF + response reflection + props exfiltration, which needs no authentication and no victim interaction.

The arithmetic defect is exactly as described and I verified it line by line. `readVarint` accumulates with `result += (byte & 0x7f) * shift; shift *= 128`, all in doubles. `128^n` exceeds Number.MAX_VALUE once 7n > 1024, i.e. at n = 147, so after 147 continuation bytes `shift === Infinity`. A following `0x80` byte then computes `(0x80 & 0x7f) * Infinity === 0 * Infinity === NaN`, and `result` is NaN from then on (a terminator byte with payload 0 returns NaN; a terminator with a nonzero payload returns Infinity instead). At `imageCodec.ts:96` the guard is `if (cursor.i + nameLen > buf.length) return null`; `NaN > x` is false, so the guard provably cannot reject a NaN length — a real, demonstrable logic defect in a bounds check. I also confirmed the Infinity branch is safe (`cursor.i + Infinity > buf.length` is true → null) and that the existing tests only cover the short-overrun and truncated-varint cases (`unpackImageRequest(new Uint8Array([HAS_SIZE, 100]))` and `[HAS_SIZE, 0x80]`), not the overflow. I agree with the finding's own honest assessment of impact: Node/Bun's `fromArrayBuffer` coerces a non-positive/NaN `length` to 0 (`length = +length; if (length > 0) {...} else { length = 0 }`), so `size` becomes '' and `cursor.i` becomes NaN, making `srcRest` empty too; the outcome is `{src: 'http://'}` and a downstream 400, not an out-of-bounds read or memory disclosure. Reachability is also narrower than the finding implies: the varint only runs past byte 1, and every token shape I could find whose plaintext is reachable here (devalue island props starts `[{`, captcha/clearance JSON starts `{"`) terminates the varint on the second byte because its high bit is clear, so you would need a payload with 148+ consecutive high-bit-set bytes sealed under a reproducible AAD. So: a real defect worth fixing as defense-in-depth behind the F1/F7 confusion, correctly filed as a BUG rather than a vulnerability, and the finding does not overclaim.

Verified by exhaustive grep: `maxPixels`, `fetchTimeoutMs`, `maxResponseBytes`, `timeToStale` and `timeToEvict` are validated nowhere in the framework. `config.ts` throws only four errors (lines 15, 40, 44, 48 — dimensions, format-in-outputFormats, quality finiteness, rotate finiteness), and the five fields named in the finding are passed through verbatim at L63/78/101/102/103/104. The consumers are as claimed: `resize.ts:52` does `new Image(input, { maxPixels: size.maxPixels, autoOrient })` and `resize.ts:144` the same for placeholders; `fetchSource.ts:71` does `AbortSignal.timeout(opts.fetchTimeoutMs)`; `fetchSource.ts:117/121` use `maxResponseBytes` for both the Content-Length pre-check and the streaming cap; `config.ts:129-130` feeds timeToStale/timeToEvict into `ImageCache` as minTimeToStale/maxTimeToLive and `imageEndpoint.ts:37-41` into Cache-Control. The ordering claim is right too: `imageCacheControl` computes `swr = Math.max(0, floor((evict - stale)/1000))`, so `timeToStale > timeToEvict` clamps SWR to 0 but still advertises the larger `max-age`, i.e. a browser caches longer than the server retains the entry. The `maxPixels` weakening is the one claim that rests partly on Bun's internals: Bun's docs describe it as 'Reject if width*height > this', and `w*h > NaN` is false, so a NaN (e.g. `Number(process.env.MAX_PIXELS)` on an unset var) plausibly disables the decompression-bomb guard — I could not verify Bun's own coercion/validation statically, but the missing validation on Mochi's side is unambiguous regardless. `AbortSignal.timeout` likewise turns NaN into 0 (instant abort → every source fetch 502s) and a negative into a thrown RangeError/TypeError that escapes `ImageError` handling and surfaces as a generic 500. So this is a genuine, internally inconsistent missing-validation gap — correctly rated BUG, since it needs operator misconfiguration and is not independently exploitable.

The factual core is confirmed. `types.ts:111` states the constraint as mandatory ('Disk cache directory. Must NOT be under `publicDir`.'), and a repo-wide grep for `cacheDir` returns only six non-test sites — `imageCache.ts:118/124/166`, `config.ts:91/128/141`, `types.ts:112/149` — none of which sees `publicDir`. Nothing in `Mochi.ts`, `runtime/publicDir.ts` or `cli/build.ts` compares the two, in stark contrast to `runtime/staticDirs.ts`, which throws on seven separate mount problems including a prefix inside the asset prefix. The disclosure mechanics also hold: `FileStorage` writes `<sha256(key)>.json` (cache-storage.ts:330/537) wrapped in a `KeyedEnvelope` that deliberately stores the plaintext `__mochiKey` so `keys()` can enumerate (documented at line 69, read at 406), and with `offloadBinary: true` (imageCache.ts:166) the raw bytes go to `<sha256(key)>/<sha256(bytes)>.bin`; so computing `sha256('MochiImage:Original:' + candidateSrc)` both confirms a guessed source and yields the blob pointer to the full original bytes, bypassing `safeOriginalContentType`. I am downgrading to BUG rather than MEDIUM for two reasons. First, there is no exploit without the operator doing the one thing the option's own docstring forbids — the mitigation here is documentation, which is why I am not calling it a false positive, but it is also why it is not a live vulnerability in any supported configuration. Second, the exposure window is narrower than stated: `resolvePublicFiles`/`registerPublicRoutes` scan and register once at boot (Mochi.ts:1831), so in production only cache files already on disk at startup become routes — the attack needs a persisted cacheDir surviving a restart, not the default ephemeral `./.mochi/image-cache`; the live dev watcher is the only path that picks up newly written entries. The recommendation (resolve both to absolute paths and throw from `Mochi.serve()` and the build CLI, mirroring `staticDirs.ts`) is correct and cheap, so this is worth fixing as a boot-validation gap.

Each mechanical claim verified. `readWithMaxSize` pushes every chunk into a `chunks` array and then `Buffer.concat(chunks)` (fetchSource.ts:127/135), so peak resident bytes per cold fetch really is ~2x `maxResponseBytes` (2x20 MB default) before the buffer reaches `new Bun.Image(input, { maxPixels })`; per Bun's own docs a decode is 4 bytes/pixel, so each concurrent decode can add up to 200 MB at the 50 MP default — if anything the finding understates the memory figure. I grepped the image and cache subsystems for any semaphore/concurrency limiter and found none: the only coordination is `MochiCache`'s per-key `inflight` Map (cache.ts:106/349) plus the cross-process `mochi:inflight:` marker, which coalesces identical keys and does nothing about distinct ones. `FileStorage` is constructed with `{ maxAge: timeToEvict, purgeInterval: 0, offloadBinary: true }` and has no total-bytes budget anywhere in cache-storage.ts — only the age-based `sweep()` the hourly janitor drives. The route-bypass claim is the strongest part and is solid: the image handler is a raw `bunRoutes` entry (Mochi.ts:1707) that never calls `buildRequestContext`, `RouteKind` has no `image` member in `KIND_POLICY`, and `checkRouteLimit` is only invoked inside the page (Mochi.ts:981) and api (1211) handlers — so this endpoint genuinely cannot be covered by `Mochi.serve({ rateLimit })` and must be fronted by a reverse proxy. The exploitability precondition is real and I want it stated plainly: an attacker cannot mint tokens, so the reachable `src` set is whatever the app published — and replaying published URLs coalesces and warms after one fetch. The unbounded-distinct-src amplification needs an app that mints from user input, which `packages/docs/148-images.md` (the danger Callout, ~line 262) explicitly blesses. That is a supported, documented configuration, and in it the attack is unbounded in memory and in retained disk (N x 20 MB for `timeToEvict`, 1 day) with no framework-level throttle available, so MEDIUM is appropriate. The 'N distinct URLs after a cold deploy' variant is self-inflicted load rather than an attack and I would not lean on it.

All three sites are exactly where the finding says and the asymmetry is unmistakable. The redirect-follow path carefully does `await res.body?.cancel()` at L105 before continuing, while: L102-104 throws `ImageError(502, 'Too many redirects')` with the final 3xx response's body untouched; L109 `break`s out for a 3xx that carried no `Location`, landing at L112-114's `if (!res.ok) throw` with the body intact; and L117-119's Content-Length pre-check throws before `readWithMaxSize` is ever entered, so no async iterator is ever created over `res.body`. I also confirmed the finding's own carve-out is right — `readWithMaxSize`'s L130-132 throw is an abrupt completion inside `for await (const chunk of res.body ?? [])`, which invokes the async iterator's `return()` and cancels the stream (`values()` defaults to `preventCancel: false`). The secondary claim is correct too: `new URL(location, resolved.url)` at L106 is unguarded, so a malformed `Location` escapes as a bare `TypeError`, which neither `fetchImageSource` nor the endpoint's `err instanceof ImageError` checks catch, surfacing as a generic 500 'Image processing failed' instead of a 502. One mitigating factor the finding omits, which is why I keep this at BUG rather than treating the DoS framing at face value: a single `AbortSignal.timeout(opts.fetchTimeoutMs)` (L71) is passed to every `fetch` in the chain, so when it fires (10 s default) the abort propagates to the still-open fetch and errors its body stream. The leak is therefore bounded to roughly `fetchTimeoutMs` per request rather than persisting until GC, so 'a sustained request stream accumulates sockets/buffers' overstates it. The defect itself — three exits that abandon a live body on a path reachable from attacker-influenced upstreams — is real, cheap to fix, and the suggested `fail()` helper or `try/finally` is the right shape.

This is the same vulnerability as F1, described from the crypto half of the chain (missing purpose label in the AAD) rather than the codec half (missing type tag). Because the duplicate verdict is only valid within a single file and these are two different files (`imageCrypto.ts` vs `imageCodec.ts`), it gets its own real verdict — and everything it asserts is independently verified. `encryptImageRequest`/`decryptImageRequest` bind only the bare `filename` (L15/L19); `payloadCrypto.sivKey()` derives one 64-byte key from `HMAC-SHA512(secretKey, 'mochi-payload-aes-siv-v1')` shared by image requests, island props (`aad: componentName`), captcha (`aad: 'mochi-captcha'`), clearance (`aad: 'mochi-protection'`) and anything an app seals with the exported `encryptPayload()`; the sealed plaintext is only `flags(1) || payload`, carrying no purpose discriminator; and the endpoint lets the client choose the AAD outright (`imageEndpoint.ts:74` → L82). The concrete instance is the one I confirmed for F1: `component-name` and `signed-props` are both printed in the page HTML by `svelteAstPreprocess.ts`, `islandIdentity()` keeps the island key a bare `\w+` token and therefore a legal path segment, and the devalue plaintext reinterprets as `original: true` + a 123-byte garbage size + `src = 'http://' + plaintext.slice(125)`. Both consequences are real: the 400-vs-403 split is a cross-purpose confirmation oracle (verified to work for captcha tokens, whose ~78-byte plaintext clears the offset; it does NOT work for clearance tokens, whose ~31-byte plaintext makes `unpackImageRequest` return null and the response identical to a decrypt failure), and where a controllable string prop lands at the computed offset the server fetches an attacker-chosen host and reflects the body, exfiltrating the rest of the sealed props into the attacker's access log — contradicting both `148-images.md:17` and the Callout at ~line 92 that names `mochi:defer` as the way to keep a `src` secret. The `aadComponents` note is also accurate (`return aad ? [...] : []` silently drops an empty-but-present AAD) and correctly flagged as a hardening gap rather than an exploit, since `slugifyStem` falls back to `'image'` so the minter never produces an empty filename. I am leaving the severity at MEDIUM deliberately: the HIGH already sits on F1 for the same chain, and raising this too would double-count one defect. Both halves of the recommended fix (a purpose-prefixed AAD, or better a per-purpose HMAC label in `sivKey()`, plus a filename-shape check before the AAD is used) are needed.

Confirmed against both the code and Bun's own documentation, which I read rather than assumed. Bun's `/docs/runtime/image` page says of `maxPixels`: 'Reject if width*height > this. Checked after reading the header, before allocating the pixel buffer' — unambiguously an input-side guard — and adds 'A decoded image takes 4 bytes per pixel'. `resize.ts` passes it only to the constructor (L52, and L144 for placeholders) and nothing anywhere bounds the output. The same page documents `img.resize(800)` as 'width 800, keep aspect ratio', which is exactly the `pipe.resize(width, undefined, resizeOpts)` call at L85 for a width-only size; and `withoutEnlargement: p.withoutEnlargement ?? false` (config.ts:55) leaves upscaling on by default, so the amplification is not clipped at the source dimensions. The height-only path at L75-77 is no safer: the width is derived as `meta.width * (height / meta.height)` with no cap, and because the `fit: 'inside'` box is itself derived from that ratio, 'inside' does not constrain the result. So a 1 x 100,000 px source — a few hundred bytes, only 100k pixels, far under the 50 MP default — becomes 1600 x 160,000,000 under the canonical documented `{ width: 1600 }`. The one thing I could not settle statically is the exact failure mode: whether libvips/Bun refuses the resize, whether a ~1 TB allocation is rejected by the allocator heuristic, or whether the process is OOM-killed. That matters less than it looks, because the attacker can tune the ratio down to the band that succeeds — a 1 x 500 source at `{ width: 1600 }` is 1600 x 800,000 ≈ 1.28e9 px ≈ 5 GB, large enough to exhaust a typical container and small enough to be allocated — so 'unbounded output allocation driven by input the guard does not cover' is correct even if the headline 1 TB figure resolves to a caught encode error. Reachability needs the transformed source's *bytes* to be third-party controlled (remote avatar, partner CDN, or the user-supplied-`src` pattern the docs bless), which is a real but app-dependent precondition, so MEDIUM is right. The sharpest part of the finding is that `maxPixels` is the exact knob `types.ts:76/123` and the docs point operators at for untrusted input, and a fully hardened `maxPixels` does not stop this — an output budget is genuinely missing.
